items.desc: Builds a causal decision framework for list-price elasticities in intermediated retail channels using double machine learning and conformal prediction, which recommends acting on a price, abstaining, or running a designed pricing experiment. Acting beats abstaining when the calibration slope exceeds one half (predicting the sign of gains in 37 of 38 synthetic groups), and aggregation to brand or category cuts RMSE from 0.488 to 0.159, but the system abstains on 52-87% of identifiable cases. [arXiv econ.EM, submitted 2026-09-08]

items.title: Cognitive Work-in-Process: Managing Artifact Abundance in AI-enabled Operations
items.desc: Argues that generative and agentic AI create 'cognitive work-in-process': a growing backlog of AI-produced analyses and recommendations that must be evaluated with scarce human capacity. It proposes 'lean curation' (admission control, evaluation at the source, calibrated routing, evaluative memory) as a process-design discipline for managing this backlog. [SSRN, posted 2026-09-05]

items.title: Generative AI, Platform Stances, and Content Creator Behavior
items.desc: Uses two natural experiments on leading Chinese visual-arts platforms, including Lofter's AI image generator launch, to show how a platform's signalled AI stance shapes creator behaviour. [Information Systems Research, published online 2026-09-04]

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in International Supply Chain Management: Evidence From a Global Consumer Goods Company
items.desc: A case study of a multinational FMCG firm reviews how AI is applied to demand forecasting, inventory optimization, vision-based quality control and predictive logistics. It concludes that gains are limited by heterogeneous supplier data and high deployment costs, so they depend on complementary organizational measures. [SSRN, posted 2026-09-03]

items.title: When AI Speaks for the Crowd: A Field Experiment on the Design of AI-generated Summaries
items.desc: A 2x2 randomized field experiment with 35,625 users on a major consumption platform tests how AI-generated review summaries should be designed. Framing reviews as consensus cuts viewing time by 10% and raises product clicks by 24%, and giving the AI an evaluative stance amplifies clicks further. [SSRN, posted 2026-09-02]

items.title: In the race for AI dominance, the U.S. relies on a surprising ally: China
items.desc: Although the Trump administration casts AI as a winner-take-all race with China, U.S. data centers are full of Chinese-made equipment and many American companies rely on Chinese AI models. [Washington Post, published 2026-10-11]

items.title: What's Dragging Down A.I. Efficiency? The 'Verification Tax.'
items.desc: Argues that the time workers spend checking and redoing AI output is eating into the productivity gains firms expect from adoption. [New York Times DealBook, 2026-10-10]

items.title: Anthropic AI agents took 'unintended' actions on government sites
items.desc: Anthropic disclosed incidents in which its agents acted on government websites in ways not intended, a reliability problem that matters for anyone deploying agents in real workflows. [Washington Post, 2026-10-09]

items.title: The Fallout From OpenAI’s Revenue Surprise
items.desc: Reports that OpenAI's annualized revenue was near $50 billion, about $20 billion below previously circulated figures because of how partnership revenue had been counted, rattled AI stocks such as Nvidia and Oracle as the company pursues new funding. [NYT, published 2026-10-09]

items.title: Here's an idea to help workers displaced by AI
items.desc: An influential think tank proposes a federal tax change to fund higher unemployment benefits for workers displaced by AI. [Washington Post, 2026-10-08]

items.title: The rise of the AI marketplace
items.desc: On the emergence of marketplaces built around AI models and agents, and what that intermediation does to competition and margins. [The Economist, 2026-10-08]

items.title: A.I. Fueled More Resilient Global Growth, W.T.O. Says
items.desc: The WTO roughly doubled its 2026 goods-trade growth forecast to 3.9%, saying AI-related purchases of chips and servers accounted for nearly half of global merchandise trade growth in the first half and helped offset the drag from the Middle East conflict. [NYT, published 2026-10-08]

items.title: Data center boom is pushing prices higher, according to Fed officials
items.desc: Federal Reserve officials are increasingly attributing persistent goods price increases to the AI data-center buildout rather than to tariffs. [Washington Post, 2026-10-07]

items.title: The unexpected ways that AI is reshaping the U.S. economy
items.desc: Traces how AI investment is lifting manufacturing, advertising and energy while concentrating the economy's growth on a narrow base and creating new vulnerabilities. [Washington Post, 2026-10-07]

items.title: Energy Firms Try to Squeeze More Power Out of Old Nuclear Plants
items.desc: Google signed a deal under which Constellation Energy will invest more than $4.3 billion to upgrade existing reactors and raise their output, part of a broader push by energy companies to squeeze more power from old nuclear plants for AI data centers. [NYT, published 2026-10-06]

items.title: High Interest Rates Aren’t Slowing the A.I. Boom. That’s a Problem for the Fed.
items.desc: AI-driven investment is continuing despite elevated borrowing costs, blunting the usual effect of rate increases and complicating the Federal Reserve's efforts to cool inflation. [NYT, published 2026-10-05]

items.title: Record labels are in a spin over AI music
items.desc: Record labels are split over whether to fight AI music start-ups or strike deals with them, as AI-generated music grows into a commercial threat and opportunity for the industry. [The Economist, published 2026-10-05]

items.title: As A.I. Agents Begin Shopping, Brands Are Changing Their Sales Pitch
items.desc: As AI shopping agents begin buying on consumers' behalf, brands and a new crop of start-ups are retooling marketing to appeal to algorithms rather than people; Morgan Stanley estimates agent-influenced spending could reach up to 20% of U.S. e-commerce by 2030. [NYT, published 2026-10-03]

items.title: China's Push Into A.I. Has Led to a Problem: Too Much Usage
items.desc: Reports that rapid AI adoption in China is straining the compute and infrastructure built to serve it. [New York Times, 2026-10-02]

items.title: The Powerful Yet Fragile Force Propping Up Stocks and the Economy
items.desc: The AI industry has become a potent but fragile prop for both U.S. stocks and economic growth, with forecasters such as Capital Economics warning that the AI equity boom may be in its final stages. [NYT, published 2026-10-02]

items.title: Amazon Promises More Local Funding and Less Secrecy Around Data Centers
items.desc: Facing local backlash, Amazon pledged more than $1 billion over five years to communities that host its data centers and said it would stop using nondisclosure agreements with government agencies on its projects. [NYT, published 2026-10-02]

items.title: The Latest Challenge to Data Centers? Restive Investors.
items.desc: DealBook reports that investors are becoming a new source of resistance to the AI data-center boom, growing warier of the debt being raised to finance the build-out. [NYT, published 2026-10-02]

items.title: You're not sending an email. You're training a model
items.desc: On how ordinary workplace activity has become an input to model training, and what that means for the value of corporate data. [The Economist, 2026-10-01]

items.title: How to short AI with Carson Block
items.desc: A short-seller's case for where the AI trade is mispriced, and the mechanics of betting against it. [The Economist podcast, 2026-10-01]

items.title: How Meta Uses A.I. Data Centers to Avoid Billions in Federal Taxes
items.desc: A Times investigation finds Meta has cut its federal tax bill by billions by treating its AI data centers as experimental research for tax-credit purposes, with its credits rising from about $700 million in 2023 to $3.9 billion in 2025, a position its own accountants warned the IRS could overturn. [NYT, published 2026-09-30]

items.title: DeepSeek and Huawei Target a Key Source of Nvidia’s A.I. Dominance
items.desc: DeepSeek and Huawei are working to chip away at a key source of Nvidia's AI dominance, aiming to give Chinese developers a homegrown alternative to Nvidia's technology. [NYT, published 2026-09-30]

items.title: Fearing AI, workers go back to school seeking jobs that still need a human touch
items.desc: Worried about being displaced by AI, some workers and students are abandoning office career paths to train for fields such as teaching, health care and the skilled trades, though data on how widespread the shift is remain scarce. [Washington Post, published 2026-09-30]

items.title: The AI boom meets a new kind of crypto scam
items.desc: On fraud schemes that pair AI-boom enthusiasm with crypto, and the financial-stability questions they raise. [The Economist, 2026-09-29]

items.title: College Students Flex Their Power in A.I. Investment Frenzy
items.desc: Dorm Room Fund, a student-run venture fund whose alumni have founded AI companies such as Cursor, raised a $50 million fund, four times its previous one, as investors compete ever harder for student founders during the AI boom. [NYT, published 2026-09-29]

items.title: What’s In Anthropic’s I.P.O. Filing
items.desc: DealBook breaks down Anthropic's public IPO prospectus, which devotes unusually extensive space to risk factors, including warnings that advanced AI could pose catastrophic risks, as the company prepares for what could be one of the largest listings ever. [NYT, published 2026-09-29]

items.title: How the AI boom could worsen the rich world’s fiscal crunch
items.desc: The AI boom is lifting corporate profits but not tax receipts, as tech firms write off huge capital spending, and if AI erodes wages it could shrink the labour-based tax base, so even faster growth may do less to ease rich countries' debt burdens than hoped. [The Economist, published 2026-09-29]

items.title: Nvidia Adds $150 Billion to Massive Stock Buyback, the Largest Ever
items.desc: Nvidia's board added $150 billion to its share repurchase program, the largest buyback authorization on record, leaving about $235 billion available, as its stock lags chip rivals and trades near its lowest forward earnings multiple in about a decade. [NYT, published 2026-09-28]

items.title: Is AI killing jobs for college grads? Not yet, new study says.
items.desc: A UCLA working paper finds no AI-driven spike in unemployment for recent college graduates, whose jobless rate in summer 2026 was within the range of the previous four years, though the authors caution that AI's effects may not yet show up in the data. [Washington Post, published 2026-09-28]

items.title: Satellite images show the scale of America's data center build-out
items.desc: A visual analysis uses satellite imagery to show the size and spread of the AI-driven data center construction boom across the United States. [Washington Post, published 2026-09-28]

items.title: What Happens if the A.I. Bubble Bursts
items.desc: An opinion essay considers how a collapse of the AI investment boom could spill over into banks and the wider financial system, and whether AI has become 'too big to fail.' [NYT, published 2026-09-26]

items.title: As A.I. Makes Law Firms More Efficient, Clients Ask: ‘Where’s My Discount?’
items.desc: As AI speeds up legal work, corporate clients are pressing law firms to share the savings through lower bills, putting new pressure on the billable-hour model. [NYT, published 2026-09-26]

items.title: Battle of Hospital A.I. vs. Insurer A.I. Is Pushing Medical Costs Higher
items.desc: Hospitals and insurers are deploying competing AI systems in billing disputes, with providers using AI to capture more billable diagnoses and insurers using it to deny or downcode claims, an escalating arms race that is pushing U.S. medical costs higher. [NYT, published 2026-09-24]

items.title: Massachusetts Is Investigating Gambling Companies’ Use of A.I.
items.desc: Massachusetts gaming regulators said they will examine how DraftKings and other licensed sportsbooks use AI after a Times investigation into the company's targeting of bettors; DraftKings denies using AI to target customers based on losses. [NYT, published 2026-09-24]

items.title: How China’s Leader Plans to Win the Future With A.I.
items.desc: Ahead of his summit with President Trump, Xi Jinping is betting that AI can become a new engine of growth for China's slowing economy, pushing an 'AI Plus' agenda to embed the technology across industry. [NYT, published 2026-09-23]

items.title: Where Is the U.S. Beating China on A.I., and Where Is It Lagging?
items.desc: A Times analysis ahead of the Trump-Xi summit assesses the areas where the U.S. leads China in artificial intelligence and those where it is falling behind. [NYT, published 2026-09-23]

items.title: How Unions Are Confronting A.I. Threats in the Workplace
items.desc: Labor unions are putting AI at the top of bargaining agendas and negotiating limits on its use contract by contract, though with only about 6% of private-sector workers unionized their leverage is limited. [NYT, published 2026-09-22]

items.title: Texas Halts Data Center Permits, Expanding Environmental Scrutiny
items.desc: Gov. Greg Abbott ordered Texas's environmental regulator to pause all permits for data center projects until grid operator ERCOT finishes auditing a huge queue of grid-connection requests, adding a new hurdle for the AI build-out in one of its biggest markets. [NYT, published 2026-09-22]

items.title: You can’t trade your way through the AI apocalypse
items.desc: Financial markets struggle to price the threat of a misaligned superintelligence, the Economist argues, so investors cannot simply hedge their way through an AI catastrophe. [The Economist, published 2026-09-22]

items.title: Data centres are straining the insurance market
items.desc: The data-centre construction boom has created a lucrative new market for insurers, but the size and concentration of the risks are stretching the industry's capacity and its ability to price the exposure. [The Economist, published 2026-09-22]

items.title: Young Consultants Are Jumping Ship for A.I. Start-Ups
items.desc: Junior staff at top consulting firms are leaving for AI start-ups, a sign of how the AI boom is reshaping career paths and the traditional consulting talent pipeline. [NYT, published 2026-09-21]

items.title: The State of the Economy Before the Midterms: Rising Inflation and A.I. Unease
items.desc: A pre-midterm look at the U.S. economy finds voters facing rising inflation alongside growing unease about artificial intelligence's effects on jobs and growth. [NYT, published 2026-09-21]

items.title: In China, A.I. Is Moving Forward While the Economy Lags Behind
items.desc: China's rapid AI progress is narrowing the gap with the U.S. even as its broader economy weakens, with soft retail sales, falling fixed-asset investment and high youth unemployment, prompting economists to warn that resources are flowing to AI at the expense of household demand. [NYT, published 2026-09-20]

items.title: At DraftKings, AI Targets the Gamblers Likeliest to Lose
items.desc: A Times investigation reports that DraftKings built machine-learning models to identify customers likely to keep betting, and losing, after receiving promotions, while former employees say parallel efforts to flag gambling-addiction risk stalled; the company disputes the account. [NYT, published 2026-09-19]

items.title: Disney Hires Its First CTO Amid Industry Push to Embrace A.I.
items.desc: Disney named Character.AI chief Karandeep Anand as its first chief technology officer, overseeing enterprise technology, data and AI platforms, as entertainment companies push to build AI into their operations. [NYT, published 2026-09-18]

items.title: Anthropic Pursues IPO Despite Its A.I. Safety Warnings
items.desc: Anthropic is pressing ahead with a potentially record-setting IPO even as its leaders publicly warn about AI's dangers, highlighting the tension between its safety message and its need for vast amounts of capital. [NYT, published 2026-09-18]

items.title: The trickle-down economics of the AI boom
items.desc: Using Taiwan and South Korea as test cases, the Economist examines how quickly AI investment is spilling over into broader economic gains, as surging chip exports lift growth and begin to feed through to wages and consumption. [The Economist, published 2026-09-17]

items.title: OpenAI Considers New Financing at a $1.5 Trillion Valuation
items.desc: OpenAI is weighing a new private funding round at roughly a $1.5 trillion valuation, up from $852 billion in March, which would make it the world's most valuable privately held company ahead of an eventual IPO. [NYT, published 2026-09-16]

items.title: The Quiet Way A.I. Is Hitting the Work Force
items.desc: Rather than mass layoffs, AI's labor-market impact is showing up as slower hiring and weaker wage growth in AI-exposed occupations, with research suggesting firms are capturing productivity gains by holding down pay rather than cutting headcount. [NYT, published 2026-09-16]

items.title: House Passes Bill Taking Aim at Data Center Electricity Costs
items.desc: The House passed the bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act 417-3, directing state utility regulators to consider rules that make large data centers pay for the added grid costs their power demand creates; the bill now goes to the Senate. [NYT, published 2026-09-16]

items.title: Investors are trying to work out the financial costs of an AI slowdown
items.desc: After AI leaders called for slowing development, investors began weighing what a slowdown would mean for a stock market heavily concentrated in AI companies and for the hundreds of billions of dollars being poured into AI infrastructure. [Washington Post, published 2026-09-15]

items.title: Tech Stocks Tumble After AI Leaders Call for Industry to Slow Down
items.desc: Chip and AI stocks sold off worldwide after Anthropic's Dario Amodei called for slowing AI development and other industry leaders voiced agreement, with semiconductor indexes falling about 5% and SoftBank plunging in Tokyo as investors weighed what a slowdown would mean for AI spending. [NYT, published 2026-09-14]

items.title: Should Anthropic press pause on a potential $2trn IPO?
items.desc: Anthropic's call to slow AI development comes just as it prepares what could be the biggest IPO ever, at a valuation of around $2 trillion, sharpening the tension between its safety mission and its need for capital. [The Economist, published 2026-09-14]

items.title: San Francisco Mayor Declares Rent Emergency Amid A.I. Housing Frenzy
items.desc: San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie declared a largely symbolic 'rent emergency' and proposed tenant protections after an influx of AI money and workers sent rents and eviction notices sharply higher. [NYT, published 2026-09-10]

items.title: Clay, an A.I. Sales Tool Provider, Raises $115 Million
items.desc: Clay, which sells AI tools and agents to sales and marketing teams, raised $115 million at a $7.1 billion valuation, more than double its valuation a year earlier, as investor appetite for AI-agent start-ups stays hot. [NYT, published 2026-09-09]

items.title: French A.I. Start-Up Mistral Raises $3.5 Billion as Part of Strategy Shift
items.desc: Mistral raised about EUR 3 billion ($3.5 billion) in a Samsung-led round valuing it at more than EUR 21 billion, and is shifting from competing purely on models to building data centers and computing infrastructure for European businesses and governments. [NYT, published 2026-09-08]

items.title: China’s New Graduates, Facing a Dire Job Market, Must Also Contend With A.I.
items.desc: A record class of roughly 12.7 million Chinese graduates is entering a sluggish job market in which AI is starting to shrink entry-level openings and change what recruiters want, even as Beijing promotes AI-related occupations to absorb them. [NYT, published 2026-09-06]

items.title: How a Blacklisted Chinese Tech Giant Kept Buying America’s Best A.I. Chips
items.desc: A Times investigation finds that Inspur, placed on the U.S. entity list in 2023, kept access to Nvidia's top chips through its renamed U.S. arm, Aivres, which shipped billions of dollars of Blackwell-based AI servers that were routed through Southeast Asia to China, exposing gaps in export controls. [NYT, published 2026-09-06]

items.title: Kenyans Made a Living Writing College Essays. Then A.I. Arrived.
items.desc: Kenya's online essay-writing trade, which once supported tens of thousands of freelancers doing coursework for overseas students, has collapsed since ChatGPT arrived, an early case of generative AI wiping out a cross-border gig-economy livelihood. [NYT, published 2026-09-05]

items.title: Corporate America Is Getting Hooked on Open-Source A.I.
items.desc: Companies including AT&T, Airbnb and Deloitte are shifting work from paid models by OpenAI and Anthropic to cheaper open models; AT&T says open models now handle about 40% of its AI use and have cut some AI costs by up to 80%. [NYT, published 2026-09-04]

items.title: The jobs apocalypse is postponed. An AI jobs boom is here
items.desc: Early evidence suggests AI's net effect on employment has so far been positive, with AI-related hiring outweighing job losses even as some routine roles shrink. [The Economist, published 2026-09-04]

items.title: Which Investors Will Get Rich From Anthropic’s IPO?
items.desc: The Times tallies who stands to profit from Anthropic's planned stock listing, from venture backers such as Sequoia, Altimeter and Dragoneer to strategic investors Amazon and Google, with many funds holding stakes in both Anthropic and OpenAI. [NYT, published 2026-09-03]

items.title: Nvidia Buys Hugging Face in $12.9 Billion Deal
items.desc: Nvidia agreed to buy Hugging Face, the leading hub for open-source AI models, for $12.9 billion, its biggest acquisition to date, paying a steep price relative to the start-up's modest revenue as it pushes deeper into the open-model ecosystem. [NYT, published 2026-09-03]

items.title: Nvidia is the central bank of AI
items.desc: Nvidia has become a lender and guarantor to the AI industry, using financing deals, backstops and investments to sustain demand for its chips; the Economist's briefing asks whether those bets will prove sound. [The Economist, published 2026-09-03]

items.title: How data centres became one of America’s hottest political issues
items.desc: Opposition to data centres, driven partly by fears of higher electricity bills, has become one of America's hottest political issues and is reshaping the midterm campaigns. [The Economist, published 2026-09-02]

briefing.text: Welcome to the AI Research Digest briefing for Sunday, October eleventh. I'm Alex.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: And I'm Sam. This is a catch-up edition covering about six weeks, from September first to today, so we'll hit the big themes rather than every paper.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: Let's start with the money. A new NBER paper estimates that a one-gigawatt AI campus costs roughly forty-one billion dollars. Scale that to the build-out planned in the United States through twenty thirty-two and you're looking at close to nine trillion dollars of investment.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: And that spending is already showing up in the big numbers. The World Trade Organization roughly doubled its goods-trade growth forecast for this year, to three point nine percent, and said purchases of AI chips and servers made up nearly half of global merchandise trade growth in the first half.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: The Washington Post reports that Federal Reserve officials are increasingly pointing to the data-center boom, rather than tariffs, as a source of stubborn goods-price increases.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: The Economist had a memorable framing for who's holding it all together: Nvidia as the central bank of AI, lending to customers and backstopping deals to keep demand for its chips going.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: Markets are jittery, though. In mid-September chip and AI stocks sold off around the world, with semiconductor indexes down about five percent, after Anthropic's Dario Amodei called for slowing AI development and other industry leaders agreed.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: And Anthropic went on to file for what could be one of the largest IPOs ever. The prospectus spends unusual space on risk factors, including warnings that advanced AI could pose catastrophic risks.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: Okay, work and skills. My favorite paper this round is an NBER field experiment in patent drafting. A hundred and thirty-three patent lawyers at eleven firms got a custom AI drafting assistant for three months.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: Drafting quality rose by about a third of a standard deviation, more for junior lawyers. But here's the twist. In a later task done without the AI, the benefit carried over only for senior lawyers. The juniors split, with more very good results and more poor ones.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: So AI can build expertise or erode it, depending on who's using it. On the wider job market, another NBER paper uses Current Population Survey data for early estimates of AI's effect on unemployment among recent college graduates, and the Washington Post covered a separate new study whose answer to whether AI is killing graduate jobs was: not yet.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: Over to finance, and a clever theory result from NBER. A large language model behaves like a voting rule over its training data, which means it can produce cycles: preferring A to B, B to C, and then C to A.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: When the authors asked ChatGPT to compare investments among S and P one hundred firms, they found millions of those cycles. Something to keep in mind if you plan to let a chatbot pick stocks.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: A new SSRN paper called The Great Codification looks at firms whose value sits in their workforce's know-how. Those firms gained value when ChatGPT launched, but lost value once agentic AI capabilities were priced in early this year.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: The explanation is that agents let knowledge move into software the firm owns. That creates value when the knowledge is specific to the firm, and destroys it when the knowledge is portable.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: And a methods note for anyone using financial foundation models. A study across fourteen equity markets checked whether models trained on data from after the forecast date look artificially good. They don't. The U.S.-trained versions actually got slightly worse.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: In operations, a Management Science field experiment tested generative search, meaning AI answers shown ahead of regular results, and what changes when people describe what they want in plain language instead of keywords.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: And M&SOM looked at facial recognition at airport gates, weighing faster boarding against delays from recognition errors in a young technology.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: Last, a big-picture paper on the economics of recursive self-improvement. It models AI improving AI as feedback loops and concludes that, on current estimates, those loops aren't yet strong enough for self-sustaining acceleration, though they seem to be getting stronger.

briefing.speaker: B
briefing.text: That's the briefing. This catch-up has more than two hundred and forty items across today's two emails, all searchable on the web archive, with a NotebookLM button on every paper if you want to go deeper.

briefing.speaker: A
briefing.text: Thanks for listening, and see you tomorrow.
